analysis.one_liner: Requires software that collects users' personal data to disclose it, get consent, and let users disable collection.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: introduced in October 2000 with one cosponsor, it died in the Senate Commerce Committee when the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required any software sold or given to the public that secretly collects personal information — your name, address, email, phone number, Social Security number, or credit card number — to say so clearly on the first installation screen, describe exactly what is collected and who receives it, and give users simple instructions to turn the collection off. Collection could not be switched on unless the user agreed in advance. It also let the Federal Trade Commission treat violations as deceptive practices and gave users the right to sue for $2,500 per violation, up to $500,000.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary computer users. Anyone installing commercial software would learn up front if the program collects personal data, who gets it, and how to turn that off — and no collection could run without their advance consent. Users could see and correct information collected under the bill's exceptions, and could sue violators for their actual loss or $2,500 per violation, with damages tripled for willful or repeat offenders. Software companies could only hand a user's data to police with a warrant or court order after giving the user notice and a chance to contest it.

how_it_helps.text: Requires any public software that can collect personal information — name, address, email, phone number, Social Security number, credit card number, or birth details — to post a clear notice on the first installation page, list who receives the data, and provide easy instructions for disabling collection without hurting the program's performance.
Bans turning on the data-collection capability unless the user gives affirmative consent in advance, and requires preinstalled software to deliver the same notice electronically before first use.
Treats each violation as an unfair or deceptive practice under the FTC Act, so the Federal Trade Commission could enforce the rules against software makers.

Creates a private right of action letting users sue to stop violations and recover actual losses or $2,500 per violation (capped at $500,000), with courts allowed to triple the award for willful, knowing, or repeated violations.

Gives users the right to see, correct, delete, or supplement information collected about them, and requires anyone collecting data under the bill's exceptions to keep it secure and use it only for the purpose it was gathered.
Limits law-enforcement access to user data: police would need a warrant or a court order showing probable cause, and the user must get notice and a chance to contest the disclosure.

analysis.who_pays: Software providers. Companies whose programs collect personal data would bear the cost of disclosure screens, consent prompts, disable features, and data-security procedures, and would face FTC enforcement plus private lawsuits with statutory damages. Employers lose nothing — the bill expressly allows them to keep monitoring employees' work computers — and web-based trackers are not covered at all.
analysis.who_pays_short: Commercial software makers and data collectors

drawbacks.text: The bill exempts the most common tracking tools of the era: its definitions carve out cookies placed by internet service providers, interactive computer services, and commercial websites, so the growing business of tracking people across the web would have continued untouched while only downloadable software was regulated.
Employer monitoring is expressly permitted, so workers would keep no new protection against their bosses collecting data from workplace computers.

Statutory damages of $2,500 per violation regardless of actual harm, with venue allowed wherever the software was used, could expose even minor compliance slips to costly litigation that bears little relation to the injury.

The exceptions for license verification and technical support could let software keep phoning home, and the safeguards on that data — security procedures, purpose limits — rely on FTC enforcement and lawsuits to have any teeth.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For users of downloadable software the bill offered real, enforceable protection: honest disclosure, opt-in consent, a way to turn tracking off, and money damages when companies ignored the rules. But it was a narrow bill even on its own terms — it left the cookie-based web tracking that dominated the 2000 internet completely unregulated, kept employer monitoring legal, and its per-violation damages invited lawsuits disproportionate to actual harm. It was a step toward spyware control that stopped well short of covering the whole problem.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Commerce Committee never took the bill up, and it died when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

narrative.text: Senator John Edwards introduced the Spyware Control and Privacy Protection Act on October 6, 2000, in the final weeks of the 106th Congress, with introductory remarks in the Senate record.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, which was its only committee action.
One Democratic senator signed on as a cosponsor; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed before the Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Software companies and web-based data collectors were better off: no disclosure, consent, or disablement requirements ever took effect, and users' software could keep collecting personal information without notice.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the bill's only recorded supporters were two Democratic senators, so the partisan shape of the fight never got a chance to appear.

industries.note: The bill would have forced companies whose programs collect personal data to disclose it, obtain opt-in consent, and offer a disable option, with FTC enforcement and $2,500-per-violation private lawsuits behind the rules. Its failure left software free to collect and transmit user data without notice.

industries.industry: Web advertisers, tracking firms, and internet service providers
industries.note: The bill's definition of computer software expressly excludes cookies placed by ISPs, interactive computer services, and commercial websites, leaving browser-based tracking — the dominant data-collection channel of the time — unregulated while regulating only downloadable software.
The bill carves out employer monitoring of employees' computer use within the scope of employment, locking in the existing workplace-surveillance exception rather than restricting it.
